articles.title: How to reduce LLM API costs in production by routing
articles.excerpt: The fastest way to reduce LLM API costs in production is to stop paying frontier rates for requests a cheaper model can handle: route each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. If your LLM…
articles.body: The fastest way to reduce LLM API costs in production is to stop paying frontier rates for requests a cheaper model can handle: route each request to the cheapest model that can handle it. If your LLM application is past the pilot stage, your model bill moves in a straight line with usage. Every new user, every agent step and every retry adds tokens, and you pay frontier rates whether the request needed frontier reasoning or not. Routing is the one lever that moves the bill structurally. Here is the reference architecture: three routing patterns, cost figures you can check against AWS's published rates, a decision framework for where to start, and the failure mode that quietly undoes naive cost cutting.
articles.author: Azrty

articles.title: Reading the IL View and Navigating Metadata Tokens in Glass
articles.excerpt: The C# that a decompiler shows you is a reconstruction. It is usually faithful, but it is an interpretation of something more precise: the Intermediate Language (IL) the compiler actually emitted, plu…
articles.body: The C# that a decompiler shows you is a reconstruction. It is usually faithful, but it is an interpretation of something more precise: the Intermediate Language (IL) the compiler actually emitted, plus the metadata tables that give every name, type and signature its meaning. When the reconstruction is clean you never need to look underneath it. When it is ambiguous — an overload you cannot pin down, a boxing conversion that vanished, a loop whose shape does not match the source you expected — the IL view is the ground truth, and metadata tokens are how you navigate it. This article is a tour of the IL view in Glass.NET , the free .NET decompiler.

articles.title: Finding and Killing N+1 Queries in a Rails API Before Your Users Notice
articles.excerpt: A dashboard that loads in 300 ms on your laptop and 9 seconds in production usually has the same cause: an N+1 query. With ten rows of seed data it is invisible. With two thousand orders, each pulling…
articles.body: A dashboard that loads in 300 ms on your laptop and 9 seconds in production usually has the same cause: an N+1 query. With ten rows of seed data it is invisible. With two thousand orders, each pulling its customer, its address and its line items, one request quietly becomes six thousand database round trips. This tutorial walks through how to spot N+1 queries in a Rails API, the three loading strategies Active Record gives you and when each one is right, and how to stop new N+1s from reaching production at all. You will need a Rails 7 app and PostgreSQL. The examples use a small order-dispatch domain, but the patterns apply to any app.

articles.title: A Screen-Privacy Tool Should Not Upload the Page It Protects
articles.excerpt: A browser privacy tool needs to inspect what is on a page before it can hide sensitive information. That creates an important question: where does the inspection happen? If the page contains an API ke…
articles.body: A browser privacy tool needs to inspect what is on a page before it can hide sensitive information. That creates an important question: where does the inspection happen? If the page contains an API key, customer email, account number, internal URL, or private message, sending that content to a remote service creates another copy of the data the tool is meant to protect. For screen sharing and browser demos, privacy should begin with data minimization. The safest page content is the content that never leaves the device. Detection has a data path “Automatic detection” can sound like a single feature, but it is really a chain of decisions. The extension reads visible page content. It decides which text resembles sensitive information. It applies a visual mask.

The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

articles.excerpt: Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?
articles.body: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
